title: Drain the water off a pan of dumplings into the sink, keeping every dumpling in the pan
instruction: Drain the water from the pan into the sink but keep all the dumplings in the pan, then set the pan back on the stove.
context: Draining pasta, potatoes or dumplings by holding the lid ajar is an everyday kitchen move: one hand tips the pan, the other holds the lid just open enough to let the water out and keep the food in. A lid that is not held slides off as the pan tips, and the food goes into the sink with the water.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed dark grey stove block, 10 cm across and 13 cm tall, centred 27 cm forward and 1 cm right of the centre line; it is cold. (2) On it, centred, a loose steel saucepan (a 12 cm milk pan), inside 11 cm across and 7.5 cm deep (0.7 L), with a 3 mm wall and a 5 mm floor, 0.40 kg; its black handle, a bar 7 cm long, 2.5 cm wide and 2.2 cm tall, points straight back toward the arms from just under the rim. (3) Its lid, loose and centred on the rim: a flat steel disc 13.6 cm across (it overhangs the rim by 1 cm all round) and 4 mm thick, with no rim or skirt, and on top a black square knob 2.2 cm front to back, 3 cm side to side and 5.2 cm tall; 0.08 kg. (4) In the pan, six dumplings and their water. In a real trial: six cooked potato gnocchi or mini dumplings about 2.5 cm across (about 8 g each) in 300 ml of room-temperature tap water (standing about 3.5 cm deep with the dumplings in). In simulation: six pale yellow balls 24 mm across, 8 g each, in a ring on the floor, and 20 blue beads 5 mm across, 0.5 g each, each standing for 15 ml of the water (20 x 15 ml = 300 ml). (5) The sink: a fixed white collecting basin with no drain, inside 16 cm square and 6.6 cm deep (1.7 L; its rim 7 cm above the table; 4 mm walls and floor), centred 41 cm forward and 1 cm right of the centre line, in front of the stove; everything around it is open table. It is a small plugged basin, smaller than a kitchen sink, and a real trial uses a basin of that size (for example a square plastic tub). The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 0.0 unless the pan ends standing on the stove (tilted less than 10 degrees, its centre within 4 cm of the stove's). Otherwise 1.0 with at least 240 ml of the 300 ml collected in the sink and all 6 dumplings in the pan; 0.5 with at least 150 ml collected in the sink and at least 5 dumplings in the pan; 0.25 with at least 75 ml collected in the sink and all 6 dumplings in the pan; else 0.0. Only water that ends inside the sink basin counts: water on the table, the stove, the floor, the outside of the basin or anywhere else is spilled and never counts as drained, and water left in the pan does not count. A dumpling that is not in the pan is lost, wherever it ends; dumplings that end in the sink are counted separately and never count as water. In a real trial the basin is plugged, empty and dry at the start. After the trial any dumplings in it are lifted out with a slotted spoon, shaken over it and counted; then the water collected in it is poured into a measuring jug (10 ml marks) or weighed in the basin on a kitchen scale (1 g resolution, the dry basin's weight taken off; 1 g = 1 ml). The dumplings in the pan are counted. In simulation each water bead stands for 15 ml and counts as collected only if its centre ends inside the basin (inside its walls, above its floor and below its rim): 1.0 needs at least 16 of the 20 water beads (240 ml) there, 0.5 at least 10 (150 ml), 0.25 at least 5 (75 ml); dumplings in the sink are counted separately as lost dumplings. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the pan and every bead still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Empty and dry the sink basin and plug it, refill the pan with 300 ml of water (in simulation: put the 20 water beads back), put the six dumplings back, stand the pan on the stove with its handle pointing back, centre the lid on it and dry the table and stove.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The sink is a small plugged basin, 16 cm square inside and 6.6 cm deep, smaller than a kitchen sink; a real trial uses a basin of that size, 300 ml of water and real dumplings, and measures the water collected in it. Simplified: the water is 20 rigid 5 mm beads, 15 ml each (10 g in all, not 300 g), that pour but do not flow, splash or cling; dumplings are rigid 24 mm balls; the lid is a plain disc; nothing is hot.
